lessonTitle: Plain Radiography of Bones and Joints

blocks.text: A 30-year-old falls from a bicycle and holds his shoulder, unable to lift the arm. The first radiograph is a single front view, and the shoulder looks nearly normal. A second view taken from the side shows the humeral head sitting out of the socket. The lesson is that reading a plain film is a systematic habit, not a glance.

blocks.markdown: A **plain radiograph** (X-ray) is the first imaging test for most bone and joint problems. A beam of X-rays passes through the limb to a detector; tissues that absorb more X-rays leave fewer reaching the detector and appear whiter. **Bone** absorbs most and appears white, **soft tissues** (muscle, fat) appear in shades of grey, and **air** appears black. A radiograph is a two-dimensional shadow of a three-dimensional structure, so a single view can hide a fracture or dislocation.

blocks.title: Systematic approach (ABCS)
blocks.text: A reliable method for reading a limb radiograph is: Adequacy and Alignment (correct patient, side and date; the correct view; the whole bone and the joint above and below included), then Bones (outline of each bone, cortex and trabecular pattern), then Cartilage or joint spaces (width, congruence and symmetry), then Soft tissues (swelling, fat planes, calcification, foreign bodies). Always look at the whole film, because a second injury is easy to miss after the first one is found.

rows: Adequacy and alignment
Patient details, date and side; at least two views at right angles (for example AP and lateral); joints above and below the injury; alignment of bones
Missing lateral view; displaced fragments; loss of normal alignment of a joint
Bones
Cortical outline for breaks; trabecular pattern; bone density; periosteal reaction
Lucent (dark) fracture line; step in the cortex; dense (sclerotic) line where fragments overlap or impact
Cartilage and joints
Joint space width and symmetry; congruence of articular surfaces; osteophytes
Joint space narrowing (osteoarthritis); articular surfaces no longer meeting (dislocation)
Soft tissues
Swelling, fat planes, effusion, foreign body
Soft tissue swelling over a fracture; joint effusion
blocks.caption: Systematic review of a limb radiograph.

blocks.markdown: **Why two views?** A fracture line running in the plane of the X-ray beam is seen as a thin line, but one running at right angles to it can be invisible. A dislocation can also hide: in the front view of the shoulder the humeral head may be projected over the glenoid even though it lies in front of it. For this reason limb radiographs are taken in at least two projections at right angles, and long bones should include the joints above and below to catch associated injuries, for example a fracture of one forearm bone with a dislocation at the other end.

blocks.title: Applying the ABCS approach
blocks.prompt: You are shown a front view of a wrist. Describe the order in which you would review it and what you would look for.

steps.text: Adequacy: check the name, side and date; confirm that the distal radius, ulna and carpal bones are all included and that a second view exists.
Bones: trace the cortex of the radius and ulna and the carpal bones for a lucent line or a step; look especially at the distal radius and the scaphoid.
Cartilage: check that the joint spaces between carpal bones and at the radiocarpal joint are even, with no narrowing.
Soft tissues: look for swelling over the wrist.

blocks.answer: Review in the order adequacy and alignment, bones, cartilage (joint spaces), soft tissues, and ask for a lateral view.

rows: Shoulder
Anteroposterior (AP)
Clavicle, acromion, coracoid process, glenoid, humeral head, greater tubercle, acromioclavicular joint, glenohumeral joint space
Wrist
Posteroanterior (PA)
Distal radius and ulna, radial and ulnar styloid processes; proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform); distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate)
Knee
AP
Femoral condyles, tibial plateau, intercondylar (tibial) spines, patella, fibular head, medial and lateral joint spaces
Knee
Lateral
Patella and its relation to the femur, tibial tuberosity, femoral condyles
blocks.caption: Normal bony landmarks on standard views.

blocks.title: Recognising abnormal findings
blocks.text: Fracture line: a lucent (dark) line crossing the bone with an interruption of the cortex, sometimes with a sclerotic (white) band where the fragments overlap or are impacted. Joint space narrowing: the gap between the bones is reduced because the articular cartilage, which is not visible on a plain film, has been lost; in osteoarthritis the narrowing is accompanied by osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis. Dislocation: the normal congruence of the articular surfaces is lost, so the bones are out of alignment; confirm on a second view.

blocks.title: Which finding is which?
blocks.prompt: A radiograph of an elderly man's knee shows narrowing of the medial joint space with small bony spurs at the joint margins. A different film of a child's forearm shows a thin dark line across the radius with a step in the cortex. Name each finding.

steps.text: Narrowed joint space with marginal spurs (osteophytes) is the picture of osteoarthritis: cartilage loss reduces the gap between the bones.
A dark line with a step in the cortex is a fracture line.
In children, remember that the normal growth plates (physes) also appear as dark lines but have a smooth, symmetrical pattern, so they are not fractures.

blocks.answer: Joint space narrowing with osteophytes (osteoarthritis), and a fracture line.

items: Bone is white, soft tissue is grey, air is black.
Use ABCS: Adequacy and Alignment, Bones, Cartilage (joint spaces), Soft tissues.
Take at least two views at right angles and include the joints above and below.
Fracture: lucent line and cortical break; osteoarthritis: narrowed joint space; dislocation: loss of congruence.

blocks.title: Normal variants and hidden injuries
blocks.text: Growth plates, nutrient canals and accessory ossicles can mimic fractures. Equally, some fractures such as those of the scaphoid may be invisible on the first film, so a patient with typical findings and a normal radiograph is still managed as if a fracture were present.

points: Bone appears white because it absorbs most X-rays; read radiographs systematically (adequacy and alignment, bones, cartilage and joint spaces, soft tissues).
Obtain at least two views at right angles, including the joints above and below, because a single view can hide a fracture or dislocation.
A fracture is a lucent line with a cortical break, joint space narrowing reflects cartilage loss, and a dislocation shows loss of congruence between articular surfaces.

questions.stem: Why does bone appear white on a plain radiograph?

options.text: It absorbs more X-rays than soft tissue, so fewer reach the detector
It emits light when struck by X-rays
It reflects X-rays back to the detector

questions.correctOptionText: It absorbs more X-rays than soft tissue, so fewer reach the detector

distractorRationale.b: Bone does not emit light on exposure.
distractorRationale.c: X-rays are attenuated, not reflected, in imaging.
distractorRationale.d: Air appears black because it absorbs very few X-rays.

questions.explanation: Dense tissues attenuate X-rays more strongly. Fewer X-rays reach the detector behind bone, which therefore appears whiter than soft tissue or air.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes why limb radiographs are taken in at least two views at right angles?

options.text: A fracture or dislocation may not be visible in a single projection
Because bone appears black in one view

questions.correctOptionText: A fracture or dislocation may not be visible in a single projection

distractorRationale.b: A higher dose is not the purpose.
distractorRationale.c: Bone appears white in all views.
distractorRationale.d: Plain films are used mainly for bone.

questions.explanation: A radiograph is a two-dimensional shadow, so an abnormality running along the beam or a displaced bone projected over its socket may be missed. A second view at right angles exposes the missing dimension.

questions.stem: In the systematic approach to a limb radiograph, which step comes first?

options.text: Check adequacy and alignment, including patient details and the views taken

questions.correctOptionText: Check adequacy and alignment, including patient details and the views taken

distractorRationale.b: Soft tissues are reviewed last in the ABCS sequence.
distractorRationale.c: Joint spaces are checked after the bones.
distractorRationale.d: Looking at bones comes after adequacy and alignment.

questions.explanation: Before interpreting a film, confirm that it is the right patient, side and view, and that it includes all of the relevant bone and the joints above and below. An inadequate film can lead to missed injuries.

questions.stem: Which radiographic appearance is typical of a fracture?

options.text: A lucent line crossing the bone with a break in the cortex
Loss of congruence of a joint with intact bone
Black region of air in the soft tissue

questions.correctOptionText: A lucent line crossing the bone with a break in the cortex

distractorRationale.b: Joint space narrowing suggests cartilage loss.
distractorRationale.c: Loss of congruence indicates a dislocation.
distractorRationale.d: Air in soft tissue is a separate finding.

questions.explanation: A fracture appears as a dark (lucent) line through the bone with an interruption of the cortex. Where fragments overlap or are impacted, a dense (sclerotic) band may appear.

questions.stem: A radiograph of a 70-year-old's knee shows narrowing of the medial joint space with bony spurs at the margins. What does the joint space narrowing reflect?

distractorRationale.b: An effusion may be visible as soft tissue swelling and does not narrow the space.
distractorRationale.c: A fracture would show a lucent line.
distractorRationale.d: Patellar dislocation would show loss of congruence of the patella.

questions.explanation: Cartilage is not visible on plain films, so the gap between the bones represents its thickness. When cartilage is lost, as in osteoarthritis, the gap narrows and osteophytes form at the margins.

questions.stem: On an AP radiograph of the shoulder, which bony structure forms the point of articulation with the clavicle?

distractorRationale.b: The coracoid is connected to the clavicle by ligaments but does not articulate with it.
distractorRationale.c: The greater tubercle is on the humerus.
distractorRationale.d: The glenoid articulates with the humeral head.

questions.explanation: The acromial end of the clavicle articulates with the acromion at the acromioclavicular joint. The glenoid forms the socket of the glenohumeral joint.

questions.stem: True or false: a dislocation is recognised on a radiograph by loss of normal alignment of the articular surfaces.

distractorRationale.b: A dislocation by definition involves loss of contact or congruence between the articular surfaces.

questions.explanation: In a dislocation the articular surfaces no longer meet, so the bones are out of their normal alignment. Confirming this on two views avoids missing a joint that appears normal in one projection.

questions.stem: A single AP shoulder view appears nearly normal in a patient with severe pain after trauma. What is the best next step?

options.text: Obtain a second view at right angles to look for a hidden dislocation or fracture
Discharge the patient because the film is normal
Take an image of the opposite elbow

questions.correctOptionText: Obtain a second view at right angles to look for a hidden dislocation or fracture

distractorRationale.b: A single view cannot exclude injury.
distractorRationale.c: Repeating the same view adds no new information.
distractorRationale.d: The opposite elbow is not relevant.

questions.explanation: A shoulder dislocation can be projected over the glenoid on an AP view and appear normal. A second view at right angles exposes the true position of the head.

questions.stem: Describe a systematic approach to reading a plain radiograph of a limb.
markingGuide: Check adequacy and alignment: patient details, side, date, view; two views at right angles; joint above and below included.
Review bones: cortex outline, trabecular pattern, lucent fracture line, sclerosis.
Review cartilage and joint spaces: width, symmetry and congruence.
Review soft tissues: swelling, effusion, fat planes, foreign body.
Look at the entire film rather than stopping at the first abnormality.
questions.explanation: A fixed order prevents missed findings and ensures that all components of the image are reviewed. The ABCS mnemonic provides a convenient reminder.

questions.stem: Describe the radiographic appearance of a fracture line, joint space narrowing and a dislocation, and explain what each represents anatomically.
markingGuide: Fracture line: lucent line with cortical break; sclerotic band if fragments overlap or impact.
Joint space narrowing: reduced gap between bones representing loss of articular cartilage; with osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis in osteoarthritis.
Dislocation: loss of congruence, articular surfaces not in contact; confirm on a second view.
Bone is white, soft tissue grey and air black.
Mention that growth plates can mimic fractures in children.
questions.explanation: Each finding reflects a different anatomical problem: a break in bone, loss of cartilage, or displacement of the joint surfaces. Interpreting each requires knowledge of the normal anatomy and a good-quality view.
